claim: On Oct. 5, 2026, Temu and Italy's Central Inspectorate for Fraud Repression and Quality Protection of Agri-Food Products (ICQRF) signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen protection of Geographical Indications (GIs) on Temu's marketplace.
The Temu and ICQRF agreement was signed at an event marking ICQRF's 40th anniversary.
The Temu and ICQRF agreement emphasizes prevention, with the two parties to provide sellers with information and guidance and meet periodically to develop joint initiatives.
Temu introduced a dedicated GI category within its global Brand Registry, through which rights holders and authorised agents can register GI rights for Temu's review.
Once GI rights are approved by Temu, rights holders and authorised agents can report potentially infringing listings through Temu's Brand Protection Center.
A Temu spokesperson said the agreement combines prevention, information, guidance, and "effective mechanisms for addressing potential infringements."
Dr. Felice Assenza, Head of Department at ICQRF, called the agreement "another key milestone" in ICQRF's strategy to protect GIs in international digital markets.
Dr. Felice Assenza said Temu has shown "a genuine willingness to engage in dialogue and cooperation."
The Temu and ICQRF agreement sets up dedicated points of contact for regulatory clarification, practical issues, and coordinating monitoring of activities under the MoU.
On Oct. 1, 2026, Temu added a dedicated geographical indications (GI) category to its Brand Registry Portal, available across all markets.
According to the press release, Temu's GI feature lets rightsholders submit notifications of potential GI infringements for review.

Temu said the GI feature is among its latest measures for businesses, drawing on feedback from more than 100 meetings with trade associations, chambers of commerce and start-up networks across Europe, where complexity emerged as a recurring barrier.
A Temu spokesperson said the aim is "practical tools that reduce complexity."
According to Temu's 2026 Intellectual Property Protection Report, its proactive monitoring database covers more than 15,000 brands.
According to Temu's 2026 Intellectual Property Protection Report, proactive removals of potentially infringing listings outnumbered reactive takedowns by 331 to 1 during the reporting period.
Temu said it works directly with more than 4,000 brands through its Brand Guardian Initiative.

Temu has quietly dismantled a nearly USD$1bn (£750m) network of suspected fake influencer accounts on Meta's platforms, which had been funding partnership ads targeting audiences in the UK and all 27 EU countries.

According to Online Risk Labs, a Czech research group that examined 16 months of Temu's advertising activity through April 2026, roughly 73 of the 100 accounts featuring the most Temu ads were likely fake.
The 100 accounts with the most Temu ads ran more than 1.4 million partnership ads, reaching a combined audience of nearly 17 billion views, according to Online Risk Labs.
Within days, 90 of the flagged accounts stopped running Temu ads entirely, and total partnership ad volume from Temu nearly halved, according to the report.
Neither Temu nor Meta responded to requests for comment on the fake influencer network.

Online Risk Labs (ORL), a Czech-based social media research group, found that Temu had spent nearly $1 billion funding partnership ads with influencers and creators on Instagram and Facebook, targeting the U.K. and all 27 EU countries.
ORL said around 73 of the 100 influencers with the most Temu ads were probably fake.
Fortune first exposed the network in a story published Aug. 31, when Temu was running 4,900 partnership campaigns a day.
According to Fortune, Temu "appears to have largely stopped" funding the influencer network.
By Sept. 4, 90 accounts featured zero Temu advertising, and ORL said the overall number of partnership ads run by Temu almost halved.
ORL said partnership ads in Ireland, Cyprus, Austria, Denmark, Latvia, and Slovenia ceased almost entirely, but it is not clear why.
Neither Temu nor Meta responded to requests for comment, according to Fortune.
On Sept. 16, 2026, Temu signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Cyprus Information Technology Enterprises Association (CITEA) to support Cyprus' technology and business community.

Under the partnership, Temu will work with CITEA's programmes, events, and member companies, and the two organisations will collaborate on shared communications to showcase opportunities for local merchants.

The CITEA partnership builds on Temu's Local Seller Program, which Temu introduced in Cyprus in 2025 to give eligible local businesses access to digital commerce opportunities and the potential to reach customers across Europe.
CITEA President George Malekkos said that partnering with Temu gives CITEA members "greater visibility and access to European markets."
A Temu spokesperson said the CITEA collaboration "gives us a direct line to help local businesses embrace digital channels, tap into international demand, and thrive across new markets."
Online Risk Labs (ORL) research found that 73 of the 100 creators whose content Temu boosted most heavily across the UK and Europe were likely fake.
Only eight of the 100 top creators were verified as real identities, 28 were based in Russia, 19 in China, and six in the EU or UK, according to ORL.
ORL says Ya Lili, Temu's top creator for partnership ads on Meta platforms in the UK and Europe, almost certainly does not represent a real person.
Temu-boosted posts from the Ya Lili account were viewed more than 1 billion times across Facebook and Instagram in the 16 months ending April 2026, according to ORL.
ORL estimates Temu spent as much as $962 million on similar ads across the UK and 27 EU countries during the 16 months ending April 2026, based on total impressions and average cost per reach.
ORL has filed a report with the EU's Digital Services Act regulator, asking it to assess risks linked to Temu's influencer accounts.
